options.text: Both mechanisms trigger, the job runs if either condition is met
options.explanation: GitLab does not combine only/except and rules — they are incompatible in the same job.

options.text: rules takes priority, only is ignored

question: In a rules list, what happens if no condition matches and there is no final `when: never`?

options.text: GitLab gives an error
options.explanation: No error occurs — GitLab simply applies the default behavior.

options.text: The job runs with when: on_success by default
options.explanation: If no rule matches and there is no fallback rule, GitLab uses when: on_success as the default — this is a common cause of unexpected launches.

options.text: The job does not run
options.explanation: Without an explicit final rule GitLab applies the default value — when: on_success.

options.text: The job transitions to skipped status

question: How does the logic work inside a single rules entry that contains both `if` and `changes`?

options.text: OR: the rule triggers if if is met OR files from changes are changed
options.explanation: Within a single rule, conditions are combined with AND, not OR.

options.text: AND: the rule only triggers if if is met AND files from changes are changed
options.explanation: Within a single rule, if and changes are combined with AND. The rules list itself is OR (the first matching rule wins).

options.text: changes takes priority over if
options.explanation: There is no priority — both conditions in a single rule are applied with AND.

options.text: if takes priority, changes is only checked if if returns false
options.explanation: There is no priority between conditions — they are checked simultaneously with AND.

options.text: Controlling when for individual jobs

question: A developer only fixed `docs/README.md`. Which jobs will run?

options.text: Jobs without rules:changes and jobs with the docs/**/* pattern will run
options.explanation: Jobs without rules:changes follow their own logic (if there are no rules at all — they always run). But this depends on the specific configuration.

options.text: Only jobs with rules:changes on docs/**/*
options.explanation: rules:changes compares changed files with patterns. Jobs with patterns for frontend/ and backend/ will not run.

options.text: No jobs will run

question: Why might rules:changes launch a job on the first push of a new branch even if there are no changes in the target files?

options.text: This is a GitLab bug
options.explanation: This is not a bug, it is expected behavior: on the first push to a branch there is no comparison base, so all files are considered changed.

options.text: On the first push there is no previous commit to compare against, so all files are considered changed
options.explanation: rules:changes compares against the previous state. If there is no previous commit (new branch), all files are considered new/changed.

options.text: GitLab compares against files in main on the first push
options.explanation: GitLab does not do such comparison automatically. On the first push there is nothing to compare to — all files are considered changed.

options.text: rules:changes does not work on new branches at all
options.explanation: It works, but behaves specially — considers all files changed on the first push.

question: Which variable allows you to determine if there are open MRs for the current branch?

options.text: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
options.explanation: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID is only available in MR pipelines. It is not set in branch pipelines.

options.text: $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
options.explanation: $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS contains the IIDs of open MRs for the current branch and is available in branch pipelines. Used for deduplication.

options.text: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'
options.explanation: This is a condition, not a variable. Moreover, in a branch pipeline CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE will be 'push', not 'merge_request_event'.

options.text: $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME
options.explanation: This variable contains the source branch name of the MR, not the presence of open MRs.

question: You have two rules in a job. First: `if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == 'main', when: manual`. Second: `when: always`. The pipeline is launched on the feature/auth branch. How will the job run?

options.text: It runs automatically (when: always) — the second rule triggers as a fallback
options.explanation: The first rule does not match (branch feature/auth != main). The second rule when: always has no condition and triggers as a fallback — the job runs automatically.

options.text: It does not run — the branch is not main
options.explanation: The first rule did not match (branch is not main), but the second rule when: always will trigger.

options.text: GitLab gives an error due to conflict between manual and always
options.explanation: There is no conflict — rules are applied sequentially. The first did not match, the second matched.

options.text: It runs as manual — the rule with main has priority
options.explanation: The rule with main did not match (condition is false). Priority is determined by order, not by when type.

question: Your team found that every push to a feature branch creates two pipelines — branch and MR. What should you add to .gitlab-ci.yml?

options.text: Add `interruptible: true` to all jobs
options.explanation: interruptible allows canceling the old pipeline on a new push to the same branch, but does not solve the branch+MR duplication problem.

options.text: workflow:rules with a $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS check for deduplication
options.explanation: workflow:rules with the condition `if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS, when: never` blocks the branch pipeline when an MR pipeline is already created.

options.text: except: [merge_requests] in every job
options.explanation: except is deprecated syntax. Moreover, this does not solve the duplication — the branch pipeline will still run.

question: What does rules:exists do in the context of determining project type?

options.text: Checks if a file changed in the last commit
options.explanation: File changes are checked by rules:changes. Exists only checks for the presence of a file in the repo, regardless of changes.

options.text: Checks for the existence of an artifact from the previous stage
options.explanation: Artifacts are a separate mechanism. rules:exists works with files in the repository.

options.text: Checks for the presence of a file in the repository and allows launching a job only for projects of the right type
options.explanation: rules:exists looks into the repository. The presence of Dockerfile, package.json, go.mod, or Chart.yaml allows automatically determining the project type and launching the appropriate jobs.

options.text: Checks if a file exists on the runner's file system
options.explanation: rules:exists checks files in the repository (git tree), not on the runner's file system.

question: A job should run on MR ONLY if files in `backend/` are changed. On the main branch it should always run. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: `rules: [{if: MR, changes: [backend/**/*]}, {if: main}]`
options.explanation: First rule: AND (MR and changes in backend). Second rule: only if (main without changes restrictions). The order is correct.

options.text: `rules: [{if: main}, {if: MR, changes: [backend/**/*]}]`
options.explanation: Order matters. The rule with main comes first — if the pipeline is on main, it will match. But for MR with changes in frontend/ — no rule matches, the job does not run.

options.text: `rules: [{changes: [backend/**/*]}, {if: main}]`
options.explanation: The first rule is not limited by source — the job will run on any push with changes in backend/, not only on MR.

options.text: `rules: [{if: MR || main, changes: [backend/**/*]}]`
options.explanation: This syntax does not allow setting different changes conditions for different if. changes in one rule is applied together with if by AND.

question: In which scenarios is using `rules:exists` preferable to `rules:changes`?

options.text: When the project type is determined by the presence of a manifest (package.json, go.mod, pom.xml)
options.explanation: rules:exists is the right tool for determining project type by the presence of a manifest file.

options.text: When you need to react to changes in src/ since the last commit
options.explanation: This is a task for rules:changes, not exists. Changes compares against the previous commit.

options.text: When you need to launch a helm deployment only for projects with a chart
options.explanation: Checking for the existence of helm/Chart.yaml via exists is a classic pattern for conditional helm deployment.

options.text: When you need to launch a docker build only if the repo has a Dockerfile
options.explanation: exists is ideal for checking for a configuration file. If Dockerfile exists — the project supports Docker builds.
